sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Mandatory Declaration**: Every printer and publisher was legally required to declare their name, place of residence, and the location of the printing press before a magistrate.
• **Deposit Requirement**: The Act mandated that a specific number of copies of every book or newspaper published in British India be delivered to the government free of cost.
• **State Surveillance**: The primary objective was to create a **centralized repository** of information to track the content, authorship, and circulation of political literature.
• **Bureaucratic Control**: It shifted the focus from pre-censorship to **post-publication accountability**, making it easier for the state to prosecute seditious content.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Prelims: Focus on the 'mandatory' nature of declaration.
Submission of free copies to the government.
Mains: Used as evidence of colonial 'intellectual policing'.

items.definition: The legal requirement to print the name of the printer and the place of publication on every book/newspaper, ensuring traceability.
The role of the District Magistrate in receiving declarations, acting as the primary interface between the press and the colonial state.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Information Gathering**: Enabled the state to build a database of nationalist writers and publishers.
• **Legal Precedent**: Served as the foundational framework for subsequent, more draconian acts like the Vernacular Press Act (1878).

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Suppression of free speech and harassment of small-scale vernacular publishers.
• **Solutions**: The eventual repeal and evolution into modern press registration laws post-independence.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'R-I-D' (Registration, Identity, Deposit).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Registration (Act 1867) requires Identity (of printer) and Deposit (of copies).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 1867 Act with the 1878 Vernacular Press Act. Remember: 1867 is about 'Registration/Record-keeping', while 1878 is about 'Censorship/Confiscation'.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Bureaucratic Surveillance' to describe how the 1867 Act functioned as a tool of soft-power control before the introduction of hard-power censorship.

keyTakeaways: The 1867 Act was primarily a regulatory and surveillance tool, not an outright ban.
It established the legal requirement for printers to declare their identity, facilitating state tracking.
It set the administrative stage for the more repressive press laws of the late 19th century.
